newsitem.title: UK: Iveco-Ford says shuts UK truck plant.
newsitem.headline: Iveco-Ford says shuts UK truck plant.

text.p: British commercial vehicle company Iveco-Ford, controlled by majority partner Iveco of Italy and co-owned by U.S giant Ford Motor Corp, confirmed on Friday that it would be shutting its sole assembly plant at Langley, near London, with the loss of 450 jobs.

Nigel Emms, external relations manager, said the decision followed a strategic production review of Fiat Spa -owned Iveco's European manufacturing plants in the light of continued overcapacity across the industry.

Emms said the announcement, which had been anticipated in the British press overnight, would mean that all manufacturing of the Cargo and SuperCargo range of trucks would be transfered to Brescia, northern Italy.

These vehicles are in the so-called medium weight segment of the market and, according to Iveco, the recession across the truck market since the late 1908s has hit this sector especially hard at the same time as European capacity has increased.

"The west European truck market is not showing signs of increase and is polarising at the heavy and light end; the medium weight segment shows a downward trend of 40 percent in 20 years," Iveco Ford Truck's chairman Alan Fox said in a statement.
Langley was the main asset of the Iveco-Ford venture when it was established in 1986. Prior to that it had been a Ford commercial vehicle plant since 1960.
Production will cease at the end of May. Emms said the factory had assembled just 7,700 trucks in 1996 compared with 18,000 in 1988, adding there was no sign of a recovery towards that peak level.
By comparison, the plant at Brescia is the main manufacturer of Iveco medium segment trucks, including the Ford-badged Cargo.
Emms said that factory had produced 16,000 of the vehicles last year, compared with its installed capacity of 36,000.
"This cuts out ths distribution chain (sending components to Langley) and makes us more efficicent. The battleground is that of unit cost, therefore we have to look at cost reduction," he said.
He characterised the decision to close Langley as an Iveco one, and made clear that Iveco had the management control of the Iveco-Ford venture "and always has had".

Although Brescia would be getting more work on the Cargo range, Emms noted, the Italian plant was not expected to gain any more jobs because another part of its production, that of cabs for Fiat's Daily range, is going to be moved elsewhere.
"The truck market is much more competitive than the car market at present," he added.

Earlier this month Ford said it had decided to discontinue current model production at its Halewood car plant in northwest England. That decision could lead to the loss of up to 1,300 jobs unless alternative production opportunities can be found.
